text: [calm, conversational] Your twenty thirty-seven has already started. This is one day of it. A Tuesday. Superintelligence has been here for years.

[calm, conversational] Six-fifteen, in your kitchen. Your phone buzzes. A message from your clinic.
Overnight, an A.I. read your scan. It found something. Early. Early enough to stay small.
[thoughtful] It wasn't luck. The same machines could have sent that warning only to people who pay extra.
So why did it go well?

[calm, conversational] You open the scan. There it is: a spot, smaller than a grain of rice.
The mind that found it has seen more scans than every doctor in history put together.
Last night, while you slept, it held yours up against all of them.

[softly] Your heart should be racing. It isn't.
These days, "we found something" is good news.
It means early. A short procedure, a few quiet days, and then it's over.
No bill. No upgrade offer. Everyone in your city gets the same careful look.
[thoughtful] Somebody decided that.

[warmly] You put the kettle on...
A whole illness just didn't happen to you, and you're making tea.
[wry] From the next room comes the sound of your kid losing an argument. With a genius.

[calm, conversational] Seven-thirty. She's still at it, at the kitchen table, in her pajamas.
Her tutor is a voice that belongs to her alone.
It knows when she's bored, when she's bluffing, which jokes make her laugh.
It also knows more physics than any professor alive.

[wry] This morning, it's black holes. She wants the answer. It won't give it.
It asks her a question instead. Then another. She groans... It waits.
[thoughtful] It isn't being difficult. It was built this way. It has never once just handed her an answer.
Why would anyone build a genius that keeps its answers to itself?
[calm, conversational] She stomps off to school without one. She won't be the only one kept waiting today.

[calm, conversational] Nine o'clock. The flat is quiet. You skim the morning news.
A new antibiotic, for a germ that shrugged off every other drug.
A treatment for a disease so rare that only a few hundred children on Earth have it.
Both designed overnight.
[wry] You barely look up. Breakthroughs have become like weather.

[thoughtful] Every night, while the city sleeps, minds that never tire read everything ever written about a disease.
They form a hunch. They test it a thousand different ways before sunrise.
Science works the night shift now.

onscreen.text: Already in use · USA, 2025 · one AI research run reads about 1,500 studies
onscreen.after: [thoughtful] Every night, while the city sleeps, minds that never tire read everything ever written about a disease.

text:
[calm, conversational] And yet none of it reaches a single patient until outside testers have checked it.
People who don't work for the makers. In the open. Sometimes for months.
[thoughtful] Some people hate the wait. Every month, they say, costs lives. They're not wrong.
So with minds this fast, why are we still this patient?
[calm, conversational] Meanwhile, another mind has spent the whole morning with your money.

[calm, conversational] Noon. Your agent checks in.
The procedure is booked for Thursday. The clinic has everything it needs.
You haven't seen a single form.
Before it pays the deposit, it asks. It always asks before it spends your money.

onscreen.text: Already being built · UK, 2026 · an AI assistant for government services; agents planned to confirm every step with you
onscreen.after: The procedure is booked for Thursday. The clinic has everything it needs.

text:
[calm, conversational] Then it brings up your health insurance.
While you were making lunch, it read every plan on the market. There's a cheaper one that covers just as much.
[thoughtful] The company that built your agent would earn more if you stayed where you are.
It tells you anyway.

[calm, conversational] It's like carrying the sharpest lawyer on Earth in your pocket. One nobody can buy.
It isn't being kind. It isn't allowed to put anyone ahead of you.
[curious] So who made it answer to you, and not to them?
[softly] There's one job you won't hand it. Telling your dad.

[warmly] Four o'clock. You walk over to your dad's place, two streets away.
He's out on the balcony, arguing about tomatoes with his neighbor. In Arabic. [wry] He doesn't speak a word of it.
His earbuds translate every sentence. And they let him hear it.
For years, he just nodded along to things he couldn't hear.
Now he interrupts people again. Including you.
You came to tell him about the scan. You can't get a word in.

onscreen.text: Already in use · India, 2025 · live translation into any headphones, free
onscreen.after: He's out on the balcony, arguing about tomatoes with his neighbor. In Arabic. [wry] He doesn't speak a word of it.

onscreen.text: Already in use · USA, 2024 · everyday earbuds cleared as hearing aids
onscreen.after: His earbuds translate every sentence. And they let him hear it.

text:
[warmly] He's eighty-two and still lives in the flat you grew up in.
The flat itself keeps an eye on him, so he never had to move into a home.
On your way out, you notice: his neighbor has the same earbuds.
So does the student downstairs, who is always broke.
The good version of everything, for everyone in the building.

[thoughtful] The best version of anything usually goes to whoever pays the most. Not here.
Why not?

[softly] Seven o'clock. Back home, dinner at the kitchen table.
Your kid explains black holes to you with a pea, a spoon and a lot of waving.
She gets every part of it right. Her tutor never told her a thing.
Then she pulls out her homework. One question, and her tutor wouldn't answer it. She has to ask you.

[softly] "Why did it go well?" she reads. Then she looks up. "Wasn't it always like this?"
She has never known anything else.
"No," you say. "It almost went another way."
"Because the machines weren't smart enough?"
"They were plenty smart. The question was who they'd work for.
Some people saw it clearly, even back then. Look."
You put an old recording up on the wall.

name: Bruce Schneier
label: ORIGINAL FOOTAGE · Bruce Schneier, 2026
text: Every AI can do both. It is a power-enhancing technology. Enhances the power of who wants to use it. So, we get to decide how to do this.

[softly] "When you were a baby, it could have gone like this.
Good check-ups only for people who paid extra. Tutors that just spat out answers. Agents that worked for the shop, not for you."
She looks at you like you're making it up. "So why didn't it?"
"Because people got stubborn about a few things."

[softly] "There was a new antibiotic in the news this morning," you say. "Nobody gets it for months."
"That's so slow."
"On purpose. Back then, those research machines were brilliant, and about one in five of their findings didn't hold up."
"One in five?"
"One in five. And you can't take a pill back.
So people insisted: test it before you trust it. Outside the companies, in the open.
Not just the medicines. Every new machine, too, before it reached anyone."

onscreen.text: Already in the lab · USA, 2025 · AI-designed antibiotics cured infected mice
Already measured · USA, 2025 · AI research system: about 1 in 5 claims did not hold up
onscreen.after: "On purpose. Back then, those research machines were brilliant, and about one in five of their findings didn't hold up."

onscreen.text: Already in use · UK, 2025 · government testers have checked 30+ frontier AI models, some before release
onscreen.after: So people insisted: test it before you trust it. Outside the companies, in the open.

text:
[softly] "And today," you say, "the agent told us to buy the cheaper insurance. Even though its makers lose money."
"Why would it do that?"
"Because back then, most digital helpers worked for whoever built them.
So lawmakers handed the machines a very old rule: if you act for someone, you owe them loyalty.
Doctors have that rule. Lawyers too.
Here's the first time politicians heard it."

onscreen.text: Already drafted · USA, 2026 · draft bill: AI agents would owe users a "duty of loyalty"
onscreen.after: So lawmakers handed the machines a very old rule: if you act for someone, you owe them loyalty.

name: Tim Berners-Lee
role: Inventor of the World Wide Web
label: ORIGINAL FOOTAGE · Tim Berners-Lee, 2023
text: I talked about the idea of, your AI could work for you just like your doctor works for you, or just like a lawyer works for you. Then their eyes lit up.

[softly] "And if it cheats?"
"Then it loses its keys. One sentence is enough."
"Like grounding it," she says.
"Exactly like grounding it."

onscreen.text: Already planned · Estonia, 2026 · digital IDs for AI agents: "limited, auditable, and revocable authority"

text:
[softly] "And Grandpa's earbuds?"
"Same story. Back then, the good version was about to become a luxury.
So towns and countries bought it for everyone, the way they once built libraries."
"Who paid?" she asks.
"Part of what the machines earned came back to all of us."
"Was it easy?"
"No. It was close, and it took years longer than anyone wanted."

onscreen.text: Already in use · USA, 2026 · AI check on a mammogram: $40 extra
onscreen.after: "Same story. Back then, the good version was about to become a luxury.

onscreen.text: Already in use · Germany, 2026 · AI second look in public breast screening, no extra charge
onscreen.after: So towns and countries bought it for everyone, the way they once built libraries."

text:
[softly] "Then why won't my tutor just tell me things?"
"Because back then, we noticed something.
Kids who got their answers from a machine did better with it, and worse without it.
So the good tutors were built to ask. Like yours.
Here's a dad asking for exactly that."

onscreen.text: Already tested · Turkey, 2025 · plain chatbot: exam scores 17 % lower without it · tutor with guardrails: no such drop

name: Sal Khan
label: ORIGINAL FOOTAGE · Sal Khan, 2024
text: I'm here with my son, and I'd love you to tutor him on this math problem, but don't give him the answer. You can ask questions and nudge him in the right direction, but I really want to make sure he understands it himself.

[softly] "And the grown-ups practiced, too: using it without leaning on it. Teachers first. Then the rest of us."
"You had to practice?"
"Everybody did."
She thinks about that. Then: "And what did you do, back then?"
It takes you a moment.

onscreen.text: Already in use · Estonia, 2026 · AI in 154 of 156 high schools, teachers trained first

text:
[thoughtful] "Not much. Asked questions. Who checked this? Whose side is it on? Does everyone get it?
At work. With friends. Before every vote.
Millions of people did the same."
[softly] She writes it down, in her biggest letters: Because people kept asking.
[softly] One person still doesn't know about your scan.

[softly] Ten-thirty. She fell asleep halfway through a question about what's inside a black hole.
Your phone buzzes. Your dad. "You wanted to tell me something today."
You tell him about the scan. "How big?" he asks.
"Small, Dad. Really small."
You don't have to say it twice. He hears every word.

[softly] You stand in the hallway a little longer. Outside, your city is going to sleep.
Somewhere, the night shift is starting.

[thoughtful] This Tuesday didn't begin in twenty thirty-seven.
It began years before, on ordinary days, when people like you kept asking who these machines were for.
[calm, conversational] Your twenty thirty-seven has already started.
